title: The Creed's shape (CCC 190)
hookLine: three parts: Father and creation, Son and redemption, Spirit and sanctification

cards: Break a seal in two. Keep one half, and give the other to a friend who's leaving for somewhere far away. Years later, a stranger knocks at your door and holds out a jagged piece.
You take out yours and put the edges together. If they fit, you know who sent this person. In Greek, a token like that was called a symbolon.
The Catechism says it's an old name for the Creed: a sign by which believers recognize each other. Today, the shape of that piece.

teach.h: IN THE NAME OF FATHER, SON, SPIRIT.
teach.b: Day two hundred ninety-seven met the Trinity; today, how it shapes the Creed. The Catechism points to baptism.
Jesus sends the apostles out, in Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "Going therefore, teach ye all nations; baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost."
Because the faith is first professed at baptism, the Creed is built around those same three names.
So it falls into three parts: the Father and the work of creation; the Son and the mystery of redemption; the Holy Spirit, the source of our sanctification, the making holy of people.
The Catechism borrows that division from an older one, the Roman Catechism, which followed the same plan. Three things to notice.

First, it's a story as much as a list: from the making of all things, to the rescue of what went wrong, to the slow work of making people holy, ending with eternal life. Second, three parts don't mean three gods.
The Creed confesses one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and Catholic teaching holds that all three are at work in every part; the division says which work is chiefly spoken of where.

Third, the shape is useful. If you lose your place in the Creed, the turns are easy to find: one where it comes to Jesus Christ, the Son, and one where it comes to the Holy Spirit. One God, making, saving and making holy.

how: Catholics profess the Creed at Sunday Mass and at baptism, and the Catechism's first part is laid out in the Creed's order, beginning with the Father and creation, then the Son, then the Holy Spirit.

games.q: a stranger arrives with half of a broken seal and says a friend sent them. how do you check?
games.why: if the edges fit, the bearer is who they claim. the Catechism says the Creed's old Greek name, symbolon, comes from a token like that: a sign of recognition between believers.

practice: If you have the Creed in a missal, a prayer book or on your phone, read it slowly and mark the two places it turns: to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.

If not, walk the three movements on the breath: something made, the world or your own body; then something mended; then something slowly growing better, and around again. If you pray, you can name each movement to God.

wordCard.voice: The Creed's shape. Three parts: the Father and creation, the Son and redemption, the Spirit and sanctification, all one God. Today's word.
